title: One Backend, Ten Scams: Inside a Shared Infrastructure Fraud Network Targeting Kenyan Job Seekers
summary: A single unsecured backend was found powering at least ten simultaneous scam campaigns impersonating well-known Kenyan and multinational companies, exposing thousands of victims' personal data and an active fee-based fraud scheme collecting real M-Pesa payments.

timeline.summary: A phishing email impersonating a real employer's recruitment process was received and reviewed.
Review of the linked page's client-side code revealed an unauthenticated backend API.
A fee-based fake certification scheme was confirmed, along with exposed applicant personal data.
A single query revealed the backend served at least ten concurrent scam campaigns, plus live third-party service credentials.
Findings reported to affected service providers, the mobile money operator's fraud desk, and national cybercrime authorities.

impact.technical: A backend data store with no authentication on any endpoint, including a root-level export, allowed unrestricted reading and writing of the full underlying dataset for every campaign it served.
impact.business: At least six real companies had their names, logos, and recruitment processes impersonated without their knowledge, creating brand and trust exposure they did not create and could not control.
impact.individual: Thousands of job seekers had personal data exposed, including national ID numbers, phone numbers, and plaintext passwords; a subset were charged real money for a certification product that does not functionally exist.
impact.public: The pattern demonstrates how a single piece of reused infrastructure can scale one scam template across many brands simultaneously, suggesting the underlying tooling may already be reused elsewhere or resurface again.

findings.title: Complete absence of authentication on the shared backend
findings.summary: Every data endpoint, including a root-level export, was reachable without any credential or token.

findings.title: Fee-based fraud scheme confirmed non-functional at its core
findings.summary: The paid 'certification' at the center of the largest campaign could not be verified by its own stated verification system.

findings.title: Single infrastructure serving at least ten concurrent scam campaigns
findings.summary: One backend and data model powered impersonations of at least six distinct real companies plus several unbranded schemes.

findings.title: Large-scale plaintext exposure of victim personal data
findings.summary: Names, national IDs, phone numbers, and plaintext passwords for thousands of individuals were readable without authentication.

findings.title: Live third-party service credentials found within the exposed dataset
findings.summary: Valid payment gateway and email service credentials were present in the same unsecured data store as victim records.

methodology.approach: This research began as passive, incidental exposure to a phishing campaign rather than a deliberate search for a target. Once an unsecured backend was identified, all further investigation was limited to passively observing data the server returned to ordinary, unmodified requests. No credentials were guessed, no access controls were bypassed, and no destructive or invasive testing was performed at any stage.
techniques: Client-side code review of a phishing landing page
Passive observation of unauthenticated API responses
Timeline reconstruction from exposed timestamped records
Cross-referencing of recurring identifiers across data sets
limitations: No access to the operator's infrastructure beyond what the exposed backend voluntarily returned
No ability to confirm total historical scope prior to the observation window
Any actor-identifying patterns observed are investigative leads only and are not independently corroborated

disclosure.disclosureNotes: The underlying infrastructure was not operated by a legitimate organization with a disclosure program; it was reported instead to the affected third-party service providers (for credential revocation), the relevant mobile money operator's fraud desk, and national cybercrime authorities. The real companies impersonated by the campaigns were also notified so they could warn their own applicant communities.

references.title: Kenya Data Protection Act, 2019 — Office of the Data Protection Commissioner
Directorate of Criminal Investigations (Kenya) — Cybercrime Unit

seo.description: Nomad research into a single unsecured backend powering at least ten simultaneous job-scam and fraud campaigns impersonating real Kenyan companies, exposing thousands of victims' data and an active M-Pesa payment fraud scheme.
